candidates.statement: A clinical trial’s eligibility criteria (inclusion and exclusion) are essential components of the trial, 29 defining the characteristics of the study population. 4 Because there is variability in 30 investigational drugs and trial objectives, eligibility criteria should be developed taking into 31 consideration the mechanism of action of the drug, the targeted disease or patient population, the 32
candidates.context: The purposes of eligibility criteria for cancer clinical trials are to select the intended patient 16 population and reduce potential risks to trial subjects. However, eligibility criteria are sometimes 17 more restrictive than necessary, and expanding eligibility criteria to be more representative is one 18 trial design consideration that may improve the applicability of clinical trial data to U.S. 19 populations. This guidance is one in a series of guidances that provide recommendations 20 regarding eligibility criteria for clinical trials of investigational drugs 2 regulated by CDER and 21 CBER for the treatment of cancer, although many of the concepts may apply more broadly to 22 other clinical areas. 3 Specifically, this guidance includes recommendations for selecting 23 appropriate laboratory values as trial eligibility criteria to avoid unjustified exclusions of trial 24 subjects.

candidates.statement: anticipated safety of the investigational drug, the availability of adequate safety data, and the 33 ability to recruit trial subjects from the patient population to meet the objectives of the clinical 34 trial. The Agency recognizes that some eligibility criteria may have become commonly accepted 35 over time or used as a template across trials, but such criteria should be carefully considered and 36 be appropriate for a specific trial context. Unnecessarily restrictive eligibility criteria may slow 37 subject accrual, limit patients’ access to clinical trials, and lead to trial results that do not fully 38 represent treatment effects in the patient population that will ultimately use the drug. 5 , 6

candidates.context: This guidance describes general principles for selecting laboratory value-based eligibility 45 criteria, e.g., minimum blood counts, with a focus on later phase trials. Overly restrictive 46 laboratory-based exclusion criteria can adversely affect the accrual and representativeness of 47 populations in clinical trials, including cancer trials. 48

candidates.statement: Analysis of industry-sponsored trials in oncology over time shows little variation in laboratory 82 value-based eligibility criteria, suggesting that these criteria may have been carried forward from 83 early-phase to late-phase trials despite the accumulation of clinical experience – during trials or 84 after approval – that should be considered in formulating the criteria in late-phase trials. 11 , 12
candidates.context: clinical trials. 7 In oncology, many patients are older adults – a population in which some degree 70 of organ dysfunction is common. However, such organ function status does not universally result 71 in clinical consequences. Laboratory value abnormalities may also represent manifestations of 72 the underlying malignancy or comorbidities that do not otherwise preclude safe participation in a 73 clinical trial. Additionally, laboratory values may vary among healthy individuals across 74 different age groups (e.g., pediatric patients), and racial and ethnic populations. For example, the 75 Duffy null phenotype has a high prevalence in African Americans and is associated with lower 76 absolute neutrophil counts but not with greater risk of infection. 8 Laboratory-value criteria that 77 do not take these differences into account can hamper efforts to enroll a representative 78 population. 9

candidates.statement: Laboratory values should be used as exclusionary criteria only when clearly necessary to 102 mitigate potential safety concerns. Among medical therapies, substantial differences in 103 metabolism, excretion, and toxicity profiles render broad recommendations across all trials 104 challenging. Restrictions based upon renal, hepatic, or bone marrow function should reflect 105 specific, well-reasoned concerns regarding drug exposure that might result in toxicity, or organ 106 susceptibility to toxicity, based upon available data (e.g., pre-clinical data, known safety profiles 107 of other relevant products). 13 Furthermore, as investigational drugs advance from early phase to 108 late phase development, laboratory eligibility criteria should be adjusted based on additional 109 available clinical data (e.g., pharmacokinetic, safety, exposure-response data from early-phase 110 trials, renal/hepatic impairment studies, drug-drug interaction studies, etc.). When developing 111 eligibility criteria for later phase studies, appropriate efforts to broaden eligibility criteria should 112 be implemented, removing or loosening any criteria no longer justified by specific concerns. 113 Acknowledging that safety is of utmost concern, protocols should be written with an aim to 114 enroll subjects who reflect those expected to use the drug, if approved. 115

candidates.statement: • Laboratory value-based eligibility criteria should be customized to the drug(s) 119 under investigation. Laboratory value requirements should be established based on the 120 investigational drug’s mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics 121 (PK/PD), and anticipated toxicities. For instance, if an investigational drug does not 122 undergo hepatic metabolism and is not expected to cause hepatic toxicity for the intended 123 patient population, hepatic entry criteria should be sufficiently broad to avoid 124 unnecessary exclusions of patients (e.g., only excluding patients with elevations in ALT 125 or bilirubin that are multiple-fold above upper limit of normal (ULN)). Wherever data are 126 available from similar agents in a therapeutic class, previous experience should be used 127 as a guide. In some instances (e.g., programmed cell death receptor-1/programmed cell 128 death-ligand 1 checkpoint inhibitors), pharmacology and toxicity profiles are similar 129 across agents, facilitating use of comparable laboratory-related eligibility criteria, as long 130 as they are otherwise well-justified. In other instances (e.g., ALK inhibitors), each 131 individual drug may have different requirements depending on its individual PK/PD 132 profile. Importantly, laboratory value-related restrictions from earlier clinical trials 133 should not be carried forward automatically but should be modified to reflect the 134 experiences of subjects in earlier trials and in post-market use, as applicable. 135

Scientific Justification for Laboratory Tests as Exclusion Criteria 117 • Laboratory-based eligibility criteria should be only as restrictive as necessary to 137 mitigate the clinical risk(s) of concern. As an example, in clinical trials of drugs that 138 may prolong the QTc interval, low levels of electrolytes such as potassium, calcium, and 139 magnesium may increase the risk of cardiac arrhythmias. A common response to this 140 concern is to require levels of these electrolytes to be within normal limits. This results in 141 unnecessary exclusion of patients whose electrolyte levels may be slightly above the 142 normal range, even though there is no increased risk of QTc prolongation. candidates.statement: • Inter-laboratory variation should be accounted for when selecting laboratory-based 149 eligibility criteria. Broadening laboratory-based ranges for eligibility, when appropriate, 150 may be one way to factor in laboratory variation. Eligibility criteria defined by broad 151 laboratory reference-based ranges rather than specific numerical values may also address 152 this variation. 153

candidates.statement: • The impact on trial eligibility, enrollment, and generalizability should be assessed 157 when selecting laboratory-based eligibility criteria. Consider the target population of a 158 study. For a trial that seeks to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a drug in renal or 159 urothelial cancer, allowing patients with lower levels of baseline renal function would 160 facilitate generation of data that is more representative of the broader patient population 161 who would be candidates for this treatment outside of clinical trials. For a trial that seeks 162 to evaluate safety and efficacy in patients with highly advanced and aggressive cancer 163 including those with hepatic metastases, allowing greater degrees of hepatic dysfunction 164 while ensuring appropriate safety measures to protect subjects, would facilitate drug 165 development in a patient population with high unmet need. In cases such as these, early 166 studies investigating alternative dosing regimens in subjects with organ impairment may 167 be beneficial. 14 Similarly, the hematologic laboratory criteria should be carefully 168 considered and broadened where appropriate in trials evaluating products intended for 169 patients with hematologic malignancies. 170
candidates.context: B. Accounting for Potential Expected Variations in Laboratory Values 155 • Demographic differences in laboratory test results, and their implication across 172 populations, should be understood when eligibility criteria are written. Given natural 173 variations in laboratory values among people that may be associated with race and 174 ethnicity, those criteria that are included should be sufficiently broad to allow for these 175 natural variations. 15 , 16 For example, as discussed above, sponsors may consider 176 broadening the laboratory inclusion and exclusion criteria for absolute neutrophil count in 177 patients with the Duffy null phenotype. 178

candidates.context: C. Routine Reassessment of Laboratory-Based Exclusion Criteria 188 • Eligibility criteria should be adjusted based on accumulating clinical experience. 194 First-in-human trials investigating first-in-class drugs or use of novel platforms should 195 generally incorporate conventional laboratory-related eligibility criteria as a 196 precautionary measure, as the clinical pharmacology and toxicity profiles of the novel 197 drug in humans are not known. For subsequent drugs in the same class, if there is known 198 clinical pharmacology and toxicity data on drugs with similar mechanisms of action, 199 these criteria can be revised early and often. For subsequent drugs in the same class, if there is known 198 clinical pharmacology and toxicity data on drugs with similar mechanisms of action, 199 these criteria can be revised early and often. Sponsors should carefully evaluate eligibility 200 criteria, especially as the trials move to late phases, removing or reducing restrictions that 201 had been incorporated in early phase trials when such restrictions are not scientifically 202 justified and would result in unnecessarily narrowing the study population. 203
